lines.text: A block of steel sinks like a stone… but a ship made of that same steel, weighing a hundred thousand tons, floats.
The secret isn't the material… it's the shape.
Anything you put in water has to push some water out of the way to make room for itself.
And that pushed-aside water pushes back up… with a force equal to its own weight.
A solid block only pushes aside its own volume… and steel is almost eight times heavier than water. So it sinks.
Here's a one-cubic-meter block. Seven thousand eight hundred and fifty kilos… straight to the bottom.
Now take that exact same steel, and roll it into a thin plate… and fold it into a hollow tray.
Suddenly it pushes aside a lot more water… because inside, it's mostly air.
It floats… sitting only twelve centimeters deep.
And it can carry about sixty-six tons of cargo before the water reaches the rim.
A ship sinks just until the water it pushes aside weighs exactly as much as the ship.
That's why the more cargo you load… the lower it sits.
And it's why ships have a line painted on their side… showing exactly how low they're allowed to go.
Next time you see a giant ship float… remember, it's not floating on steel. It's floating on air.
